steps.title: Words → maths
steps.intro: Translate one phrase at a time — then answer what they actually asked.

head: Words
Maths
rows: The difference between A and B is 12
3 notebooks cost the same as 5 pens
The ratio of A to B is \(2:3\)

tips: Three stages: translate → solve → answer what they asked.
Long question? Work step by step — one phrase at a time.

steps.stem: Six trays hold 42 biscuits. At the same number per tray, how many biscuits fit on 15 trays?
explanation: Forty-two biscuits are shared equally among six trays, so each tray holds seven. Fifteen trays hold fifteen groups of seven, which is 105. Finding the value for one tray is a dependable route whenever a direct multiplier is not immediately comfortable.

steps.stem: At a constant pace, a student completes 12 exercises in 8 minutes. How many exercises does she complete in 14 minutes?
explanation: Twelve exercises in eight minutes means three exercises in two minutes: divide both numbers by four. Fourteen minutes contains seven two-minute blocks, so the student completes seven groups of three, or twenty-one exercises. This avoids an awkward one-minute rate if you prefer whole numbers.

steps.stem: A bakery sells a tart for 58 credits. Making it uses 300 g of pastry at 6 credits per 100 g, 200 g of filling at 9 credits per 100 g, and 4 berries at half a credit each. Ignoring other costs, what is the selling price minus ingredient cost?
explanation: The pastry uses three 100-gram portions, costing eighteen credits. The filling uses two such portions, also costing eighteen. Four berries at half a credit each cost two credits. The total ingredient cost is eighteen plus eighteen plus two, or thirty-eight.

The requested difference is the selling price minus that cost: fifty-eight minus thirty-eight is twenty. Thirty-eight is a useful intermediate value, but it is not what the question asks us to select.

steps.stem: Hire company A charges 3 credits for every minute or part of a minute. Company B charges 14 credits for every 5-minute block or part of a block. What is the difference between the charges for an 11.5-minute hire?
explanation: Company A charges for twelve minutes because the final half-minute starts a new minute. Its charge is twelve times three, or thirty-six. Company B charges for three five-minute blocks, because two blocks cover only ten minutes. Its charge is three times fourteen, or forty-two.
The difference is six credits. We round the number of billing units up; we do not round 11.5 to the nearest five or charge a fraction of the last block. “Or part of” is the wording that forces this.

steps.title: Ratios and equal ratios
steps.intro: The ratio table and the ratio facts you will use all through the course.

tables.title: Equal ratios (ratio table)
head: Situation
Method
rows: Across or down is a whole number
triangle value: diagonal product ÷ the remaining number
cross-multiply: the diagonal products are equal

tables.title: Ratio facts
head: Fact
Example
rows: No amounts from a ratio alone

tips: Give the plain \(x\) to the smaller quantity — no dividing later.
One thing is twice another? The \(\times2\) goes on the smaller side.

steps.stem: In a class, boys make up \(\frac38\) of all students. Which could be the difference between the numbers of girls and boys?
explanation: Boys occupy three parts out of eight. Girls occupy the remaining five. The difference is two parts, so it must be twice a whole-number unit count and so even. Only eighteen among the choices is even.

To confirm that eighteen is possible, take nine students per part. Then there are twenty-seven boys and forty-five girls, a difference of eighteen, and twenty-seven is three eighths of the total seventy-two.

steps.stem: The prices of a scooter and a small car are in the ratio 3:8. The car costs 15,000 credits more. What is their combined price?
explanation: The difference between eight parts and three parts is five parts. Those five parts cost fifteen thousand, so one part is three thousand. Together the vehicles cost eleven parts, giving thirty-three thousand.
The price ratio does not mean the vehicles cost three and eight credits. It describes their relative sizes. The actual money difference supplies the scale that turns each part into a price.

steps.stem: A center plans to put the same number of students in each of 6 rooms. One room becomes a storeroom, so each of the 5 remaining rooms must hold 3 more students. How many students per room were originally planned?
explanation: Let x be the originally planned number in each room. The original total is 6x. With five rooms, each holds x+3, so the total is also 5(x+3). Set them equal because moving the students does not change how many there are.
Expanding gives 6x=5x+15, so x=15. This x answers the original-per-room question. The new count is eighteen per room, which appears tempting but refers to the later arrangement.

steps.title: Give It to the Little Guy

steps.stem: Iris is 6 years older than Leo. Four years ago, Iris was twice Leo’s age. How old is Leo now?
explanation: At the earlier time, the younger age and the age gap are both one ratio unit in a 1:2 age ratio. The gap is six, so Leo was six then. Four years later he is ten.

steps.stem: A shopper has 84 credits, enough for 5 identical notebooks but not enough for 6. Which could be the price of one notebook?
explanation: A price of sixteen makes five notebooks cost eighty, which fits the budget. Six cost ninety-six, which does not. Both conditions are satisfied.

At fourteen, six notebooks cost exactly eighty-four, so the shopper could afford six and that choice fails. At eighteen or twenty, even five notebooks cost too much. The phrase “enough for” includes exact equality; “not enough for” does not.

steps.stem: One credit buys 2 oranges, 3.5 pears, or 8 plums, with costs proportional to quantity. What is the cost of 6 oranges, 5 pears, and 8 plums? Fractional credits may be paid.
explanation: Six oranges cost three credits, and eight plums cost one credit. Five pears cost \(5:3.5\). Multiply top and bottom by two to write that as \(\frac{10}{7}\) credits. The total is \(4+\frac{10}{7}=\frac{38}{7}\).
Notice that multiplying by two removes the half more efficiently than multiplying by ten. We scale both parts of the division by the same factor, so the cost does not change.

steps.stem: A selection program starts with 144 applicants. At the end of each round, \(\frac56\) of the applicants who began that round remain. How many remain after two rounds?
explanation: In round one, one sixth of 144 is twenty-four, so five sixths is 120. Those 120 start round two. One sixth of 120 is twenty, so five sixths is one hundred.
The second fraction acts on 120, not again on 144. Each round removes the same fraction of a changing group, so the numbers removed are twenty-four and twenty rather than two identical amounts.

steps.stem: There are \(\frac35\) as many apprentices as supervisors in a room. What fraction of all the people are apprentices?
explanation: Use five ratio parts for supervisors and three for apprentices. There are eight parts altogether. Apprentices so form three eighths of the total. The given three fifths compares apprentices with supervisors, not with everyone.

steps.stem: A grower sends 4 times as many pears to shops as to a market. One quarter of the shop pears and one third of the market pears are rejected. What fraction of all the pears is rejected?
explanation: We can choose the scale because only a fraction is requested. Use three market pears and twelve shop pears. The 4:1 ratio holds, and both rejection fractions now produce whole pears.

The shops reject one quarter of twelve, or three. The market rejects one third of three, or one. Four out of the fifteen total pears are rejected. Choosing one market pear would create fractional pears in the working; using three keeps the counting concrete.

steps.stem: A maker owns red and blue tiles. She gives away \(\frac14\) of the red tiles and \(\frac16\) of the blue tiles, always giving whole tiles. The remaining color counts are 9 and 20, in an unknown order. How many tiles did she own originally?
explanation: The red remainder is three quarters of its original count, so it must consist of three equal whole-number units. Nine can be divided into three such units; twenty cannot. Thus nine is the red remainder. Each quarter contained three tiles, making twelve red tiles originally.

The twenty blue tiles are five sixths of the original blue count. One sixth is four tiles, so the original blue count was twenty-four. Add twelve and twenty-four to get thirty-six. The whole-tile condition resolves the unknown order of the two remainders.

steps.stem: Club A has 3 times as many members as Club B. Three members move from A to B. Afterwards B has half as many members as A. How many members do the clubs have altogether?
explanation: Let B start with b members, so A starts with 3b. After the move, B has b+3 and A has 3b−3. B is then half of A, giving 2(b+3)=3b−3.
Solve: 2b+6=3b−3, so b=9. The original total was four b, or thirty-six. The transfer changes the distribution but keeps that total fixed.

steps.stem: A freelancer receives a fixed monthly payment plus the same extra amount for each completed task. Ten tasks bring 320 credits; six tasks bring 208 credits. What is the payment per task?
explanation: The fixed payment is the same in both months. The difference in money so comes entirely from the four extra tasks. The difference is 320−208=112 credits. Divide by four to get twenty-eight per task.
This is often the quickest route: compare what changed and cancel what stayed the same. We do not need the fixed monthly payment to answer the question, although we can find it afterwards as a check.

steps.stem: Eight large blocks and twelve small blocks weigh 1,000 g altogether. All large blocks have equal weight, and all small blocks have equal weight. How much do ten large and fifteen small blocks weigh?
explanation: Eight becomes ten by multiplying by five quarters. Twelve becomes fifteen by exactly the same factor. Because every part of the collection is scaled equally, the combined weight is scaled by five quarters too.

One quarter of one thousand is 250. Add that quarter to the original thousand to get 1,250 g. We do not need to find the separate weights of the two types of block, which the single equation would not determine.

steps.stem: Ari and Bea have 60 counters altogether. Ari gives Bea 9 counters, after which they have equal numbers. What was Ari’s original count divided by Bea’s original count?
explanation: The transfer keeps sixty counters in total. Equal final counts must so be thirty each. Reverse the transfer: give Ari back the nine, making thirty-nine, and remove those nine from Bea, leaving twenty-one.

The requested ratio is thirty-nine divided by twenty-one. Divide both by three to get thirteen sevenths. Reversing the transfer must change both people’s counts; adding nine only to Ari would incorrectly increase the total.

steps.title: General problems — toolkit
steps.intro: No formula for these — pick the tool that fits the question.

head: Tool
When
Example
rows: a rate like "1 credit buys 3.5 pears"
A : B = 3 : 5, A out of all = \(\frac38\)
the total lies between the two rates
3:1 and 2:1 → total divides by 4 and by 3

tips: Plug in the answers? Start with the case that has fewer items — easier to calculate.
Found x? Check it is what they asked before you circle.

steps.stem: A small storage box costs \(x\) credits. A large box costs \(\frac{x^2+32}{x}\) credits. The large box costs 3 times as much as the small one. How much does the small box cost?
explanation: Three times the small price is \(3x\), so set \(\frac{x^2+32}{x}=3x\). A price is positive, so multiplying by \(x\) is allowed.
This gives \(x^2+32=3x^2\), then \(x^2=16\). Keep the positive solution: \(x=4\).

steps.stem: A collection has blue, green, and orange tiles. There are 3 times as many blue tiles as green tiles, and twice as many green tiles as orange tiles. Which total is possible?
explanation: Start with one unit of orange. Green needs two units and blue needs six. The total is nine equal units, so the total must be a multiple of 9. Only 27 works.

steps.stem: A delivery drone can travel 540 km while carrying 80 g. Each extra gram reduces its range by 4 km. What is its range when carrying 113 g?
explanation: The extra load is 113−80=33 g. Each of those grams removes 4 km, so the total loss is 132 km. Subtract that loss from the original 540 km.

steps.stem: Three teams have 3, 4, and 5 members. They split a 660-credit equipment bill in proportion to team size. How much does the three-person team pay?
explanation: There are 3+4+5=12 people. The bill is 660:12=55 credits per person. The smallest team has three people, so it pays 3×55=165.

steps.stem: Mira has n whole plums. She eats 4, gives half of the remaining plums to a neighbour, and uses 3 whole plums for a dessert. Which value of n is possible?
explanation: After she eats four, the remaining number must be even so that half is a whole number. Mira must also keep at least three. Thus n is even and n≥10. Only 12 meets both conditions.

steps.stem: A reference book costs 18 credits more than a notebook. Four reference books cost the same as six notebooks. What does one reference book cost?
explanation: Let a notebook cost n. A reference book costs n+18. Equal bills give 4(n+18)=6n, so 72=2n and n=36. Add 18 to get the requested reference-book price, 54.

steps.stem: Lena donates \(\frac14\) of her earnings, then spends 180 credits. She has 720 credits left. What were her earnings?
explanation: Before spending 180, she had 720+180=900. This is the \(\frac34\) left after the donation. One quarter is 300, so all four quarters total 1,200.

steps.stem: A grower has \(x\) trays. Each tray contains \(x\) pots, and each pot contains 2 seedlings. How many seedlings are there?
explanation: There are \(x\times x=x^2\) pots. Each has two seedlings, so the total is \(2x^2\). We multiply because every tray has its own full set of pots.

steps.stem: One large battery stores \(\frac54\) as much energy as one small battery. Which pack stores the most energy?
explanation: Give each small battery 4 energy units and each large one 5. The four packs contain 38, 35, 36, and 36 units respectively when listed as: six large plus two small, seven large, nine small, four of each. The first pack is largest.

steps.stem: Five sketchpads cost as much as two folders and six pencils. A folder costs 3 times as much as a pencil. How many folders cost as much as ten sketchpads?
explanation: A folder costs three pencil units. Two folders and six pencils cost 2×3+6=12 units, so five sketchpads cost 12. Ten sketchpads cost 24 units, which buy 24:3=8 folders.

steps.stem: Noah chooses a real number \(x\), divides it by 8, subtracts 3, multiplies by 6, and adds 18. The result is \(x\) again. What is \(x\)?
explanation: The result is \(6(\frac{x}{8}-3)+18\). Expanding cancels the minus 18 with the plus 18, leaving \(\frac34x\). For this to equal x, one quarter of x must be zero, so x=0.

steps.stem: One crest equals 8 sparks. One crest is worth \(\frac25\) of a crown. How many sparks are worth one crown?
explanation: If 8 sparks make two fifths of a crown, 4 sparks make one fifth. Five such parts make a whole crown: 5×4=20.

steps.stem: A potter sells \(\frac25\) of a batch, then \(\frac13\) of the pots left. Every pot has the same price. These sales bring in 360 credits. What would selling the entire batch bring in?
explanation: After the first sale, \(\frac35\) remains. One third of that is \(\frac15\) of the original batch. In total she sells \(\frac25+\frac15=\frac35\). If three fifths bring 360, each fifth brings 120 and all five bring 600.

steps.stem: A jar contains 120 spoonfuls of cocoa and costs 18 credits. A bag contains 300 spoonfuls of sugar and costs 12 credits. What is the ingredient cost of a drink using two spoonfuls of cocoa and three of sugar?
explanation: One spoonful of cocoa costs 18:120=0.15 credits, and one spoonful of sugar costs 12:300=0.04. The drink uses two of the first and three of the second.

steps.stem: For 6 days, a camper gathers 25 berries a day and eats x of them each day. The saved berries then last 18 days at 5 berries a day. What is x?
explanation: The later supply must be 18×5=90 berries. The camper gathers 6×25=150 berries, so 60 are eaten during the first six days. That is 60:6=10 per day.

steps.stem: An older dog is 6 years older than a younger dog. Their current age ratio is 4:1. What will the older-to-younger ratio be in 2 years?
explanation: The ratio gap is three units, and that equals six years. One unit is two years, so their ages are eight and two. In two years they will be ten and four, giving 10:4=5:2.

steps.stem: One meter of silk costs \(x\) credits and one meter of cotton costs \(y\) credits. Their prices add to 17 credits, and silk costs 5 credits more. A shop sells x meters of silk and buys y meters of cotton. What is the difference between the money received and spent?
explanation: Two prices with sum 17 and difference 5 are 11 and 6. Selling 11 metres at 11 credits brings 121; buying six metres at six credits costs 36. The difference is 85.

steps.stem: Four positive numbers are arranged in two rows: a, b above c, d. The row totals are equal, and the column totals are equal. Which of the following statements is necessarily true?
explanation: The row condition is \(a+b=c+d\). The column condition is \(a+c=b+d\). Subtracting gives \(b-c=c-b\), so \(b=c\). Substitute that into either equation to get \(a=d\).

steps.stem: At the end of each of 3 months, a reserve gives away \(\frac14\) of its remaining supplies. What fraction of the starting supplies remains after the third giveaway?
explanation: Each month keeps \(\frac34\) of whatever is there at that time. Apply that factor three times: \(\frac34\times\frac34\times\frac34=\frac{27}{64}\). We do not subtract three quarters of the original amount, because the supply becomes smaller each month.

steps.stem: A manual contains 48,000 words and 40 diagrams. A leaflet contains 3,000 words and 15 diagrams. The word-to-diagram ratio of the manual is how many times that of the leaflet?
explanation: The manual has 48,000:40=1,200 words per diagram. The leaflet has 3,000:15=200. Compare those values: 1,200:200=6.

steps.stem: A workshop has 42 stools and carts altogether. Each stool has 3 legs and each cart has 4 wheels. The total number of legs and wheels is 146. How many carts are there?
explanation: If all 42 items were stools, there would be 42×3=126 legs. Each cart replaces three legs with four wheels, adding one to the count. The extra 146−126=20 so means 20 carts.

steps.stem: A festival has \(\frac56\) as many visitors as local residents. Visitors make up what fraction of all the people at the festival?
explanation: Use six parts for residents and five for visitors. The total is eleven parts. Visitors so make up \(\frac5{11}\) of the combined group. The denominator must include both groups.

steps.stem: Ada starts work at 09:00 on each of five days. On three of those days she takes an unpaid one-hour break. She finishes at the same time every day and works 32 paid hours in total. When does she finish?
explanation: She must be at work for 32 paid hours plus three unpaid hours: 35 hours altogether. Split equally over five days, that is seven hours from arrival to departure. Seven hours after 09:00 is 16:00.

steps.stem: A large kite’s tail is \(\frac38\) of its total length. A small kite’s tail is \(\frac14\) of its total length. The large tail is 9 times as long as the small tail. What is the ratio of the kites’ total lengths?
explanation: Let the total lengths be L and S. The tails satisfy \(\frac38L=9\times\frac14S\). Multiplying by 8 gives \(3L=18S\), so \(L=6S\).

steps.stem: Iris and Owen have 30 counters altogether. Iris gives Owen 9 counters and then has 4 fewer than Owen. What was the ratio of Iris’s counters to Owen’s before the transfer?
explanation: The final counts add to 30 and differ by 4. They are 13 for Iris and 17 for Owen. Reverse the transfer: Iris started with 22 and Owen with 8. The ratio 22:8 reduces to 11:4.

steps.stem: Ben borrows some money and spends \(\frac25\) of it on rice. He repays his lender with \(\frac34\) of that rice at its purchase value. He still owes 8.40 credits. How much did he borrow?
explanation: The rice used to repay the loan is worth \(\frac34\times\frac25=\frac3{10}\) of the loan. So seven tenths is still owed. Seven tenths is 8.40; one tenth is 1.20, and the whole loan is 12.

steps.stem: A tutor changes every score by multiplying it by \(\frac35\) and then adding 24. June’s score goes down. Which of the following is necessarily true of her original score?
explanation: An unchanged score satisfies \(\frac35x+24=x\). The missing two fifths must be 24, so x=60. Above 60, the amount removed exceeds 24 and the score goes down. Below 60, the added 24 more than makes up for the reduction.

steps.stem: A box of beads is split into two piles. One quarter of the first pile is used, and one sixth of the second pile is used. The two remaining piles contain 18 and 25 beads, in an unknown order. How many beads were in the box?
explanation: The first remainder is three quarters of its starting pile, so it must be a multiple of 3. That must be 18, not 25. Its starting size was 18:3×4=24. The second remainder is five sixths, so it began with 25:5×6=30. Total: 54.

steps.stem: Two studios own the same number of brushes. One shares its brushes equally among 8 artists, and the other among 24 artists. Each artist in the first studio receives 3 times as many brushes as each artist in the second. How many brushes does each studio own?
choices: It cannot be determined from the information given.
explanation: The second studio has three times as many artists sharing the same total. Each artist must so receive one third as many brushes, whatever the total is. The last sentence repeats information we already had and does not fix the number of brushes.

steps.stem: There are \(n\) players in a room, where \(n\ge5\). Each starts with \(2n\) tokens. One at a time, a player gives 2 tokens to every player still in the room and leaves. How many tokens does the fifth player have when leaving?
explanation: Before leaving, the fifth player receives two tokens from each of the first four leavers: eight tokens. They then give two tokens to each of the n−5 players who remain. Starting with 2n gives 2n+8−2(n−5)=18.

steps.stem: A school orders blue and white folders in the ratio 5:7. After 18 blue folders are added, the two colors have equal counts. How many folders were in the original order?
explanation: White exceeds blue by two ratio parts. That gap is 18, so one part is nine. The original order has twelve parts, giving 12×9=108.

steps.stem: A craft stall charges 8 credits to enter a workshop plus 3 credits per item made. Another stall charges no entry fee and 5 credits per item. For how many items are the costs equal?
explanation: The first stall costs eight extra at the start but saves two credits on each item. Four items save 4×2=8, exactly covering the entry fee.

steps.stem: A water tank is \(\frac35\) full. After 28 liters are added, it is \(\frac45\) full. What is its capacity?
explanation: The added water fills one fifth of the tank, because \(\frac45-\frac35=\frac15\). If one fifth is 28 litres, five fifths hold 5×28=140 litres.

steps.stem: Four years ago, a tree was 3 times as old as a shrub. Today the tree is twice as old as the shrub. How old is the shrub today?
explanation: Let the shrub be s years old now, so the tree is 2s. Four years ago their ages were s−4 and 2s−4. The earlier comparison gives 2s−4=3(s−4), so s=8.

steps.stem: A blend uses 3 parts juice and 5 parts water. How many liters of water must be added to 24 liters of the blend to make the juice-to-water ratio 1:3?
explanation: The original 24 litres contain 24:8×3=9 litres of juice and 15 litres of water. The new ratio needs 27 litres of water for those same nine litres of juice. Add 27−15=12 litres.

steps.stem: A train ticket costs 7 credits more than a bus ticket. Three train tickets and two bus tickets cost 81 credits altogether. What does a bus ticket cost?
explanation: If all five tickets cost the bus price, the bill would be 3×7=21 credits lower. That leaves 81−21=60 for five bus-priced tickets. Each bus ticket costs 12.

steps.stem: A museum sells 4 adult tickets for the same total price as 7 child tickets. Two adults and seven children pay 84 credits. What does an adult ticket cost?
explanation: Seven child tickets cost as much as four adult tickets. The whole group so costs as much as six adult tickets. Divide 84 by six to get 14 credits.
